plan.chapterName: OpenStax Precalculus 2e, chapter 9: Systems of Equations and Inequalities
plan.contextChunk: This figure is one graph on a dotted coordinate grid showing two straight lines and the point at which they cross. The horizontal axis is labeled x and carries integer ticks from -6 to 6; the vertical axis is labeled y with integer ticks from -5 to 5, and each axis ends in arrowheads. A blue line of negative slope enters at the upper left and descends to the lower right, meeting the vertical axis just below the origin; a blue label at the left edge reads x + 2y = -1. A red line of positive slope climbs from the lower left to the upper right and meets the vertical axis at 3; a red label at the lower left reads -x + y = 3. Both lines end in arrowheads at each extremity. A filled black dot marks the single crossing, in the second quadrant just left of the vertical axis and slightly above the horizontal axis, and the coordinates printed above it read (-7/3, 2/3) with the fractions stacked. Drawing both equations against shared axes converts the algebraic system into a picture whose solution is a location. The graph makes visible that these lines meet at exactly one point, so the system has a single solution.

interactionPlan.concept: A system of two linear equations has a solution at the coordinate point where the two graphed lines intersect, because that point satisfies both equations at once.

interactions.label: Blue line y-intercept
interactions.teaches: Changing one constant shifts an entire line up or down, so the system's solution moves because the ordered pair satisfying both equations changes.

interactions.label: Red line slope
interactions.teaches: Changing a line's slope rotates it about its y-intercept, showing that line orientation determines whether two equations meet in one point or become parallel with no shared solution.
Selecting the crossing point connects the graph back to algebra: the same ordered pair makes both equations true.

demo_steps.title: Original system
demo_steps.narration: The blue line represents x + 2y = -1 and the red line represents -x + y = 3. Their single crossing point, (-7/3, 2/3), is the solution because it lies on both lines.

demo_steps.title: Shift one equation
demo_steps.narration: Move the blue line's y-intercept. The blue line stays parallel to itself, but the intersection point slides to a new location because the constant in that equation has changed.

demo_steps.title: Rotate the other equation
demo_steps.narration: Now change the red line's slope. As the red line rotates about its y-intercept, the crossing point updates; when the lines have the same slope but different intercepts, they are parallel and have no solution.

demo_steps.title: Verify the solution algebraically
demo_steps.narration: Return to the original graph and click the black dot. Substituting its coordinates into both equations shows that the same ordered pair satisfies both lines.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: The solution to a system of two linear equations is not just where the lines cross visually; it is the ordered pair that satisfies both equations simultaneously.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Recreate the figure as a centered Cartesian grid with light dotted grid lines and black arrowed axes. The original blue line should have slope -1/2 and y-intercept -1/2, labeled x + 2y = -1 in blue near the left edge. The original red line should have slope 1 and y-intercept 3, labeled -x + y = 3 in red near the lower left. Mark the original intersection with a black dot in quadrant II and a nearby coordinate label using fractional notation. When sliders move, redraw both infinite arrowed line segments within the visible grid, update the intersection dot and coordinate label when a visible intersection exists, and replace the dot with a clear 'parallel: no solution' status when the slopes match and intercepts differ.

authoredContext:
We gain an important perspective on systems of equations by looking at the graphical representation. See the figure to find that the equations intersect at the solution. We do not need to ask whether there may be a second solution because observing the graph confirms that the system has exactly one solution.

This graph displays a system of two linear equations plotted on a coordinate plane. The blue line represents the equation x + 2y = -1, while the red line represents the equation -x + y = 3. The point where these two lines intersect, indicated by a black dot, is the solution to the system of equations and is labeled as (-7/3, 2/3). The x-axis ranges from -6 to 6, and the y-axis ranges from -5 to 5, with a grid background to aid in reading the coordinates.

discrepancies: An extra in-plot status badge reading "one solution" appears in the upper-right of the grid, which is not present in the source figure and adds visual clutter.
The intersection coordinate label is drawn inside a rounded white callout box, whereas the source uses plain black mathematical text without a box.

The equation labels are close but not identical in placement and scale; the blue label sits farther inside/clearer than the partly left-positioned source label, and the red label is slightly lower/shifted.
The generated grid and line strokes are slightly lighter/thinner than the source, making the figure a bit less like the original at a glance.
evaluation.notes: The generated graph accurately reproduces the two lines, axes, grid, arrowheads, labels, and intersection, with useful interactions, but adds a non-source status badge and boxed coordinate callout that reduce static faithfulness.
